Communication

Helping children speak English with confidence.

Confidence grows when children have something meaningful to say, enough language to begin and listeners who care more about the message than a perfect sentence.

By Princeway CollegePublished 6 November 20268 minute read

A child may understand English, complete written work and still avoid speaking. That hesitation is not laziness. Speaking happens in real time, in front of other people, with little opportunity to erase and begin again.

The most effective support reduces the emotional risk while increasing useful practice. Children need many ordinary conversations in which mistakes are expected, meaning matters and adults respond with interest.

Why children hesitate

Some children are searching for vocabulary. Others fear being corrected, compared or laughed at. A child may speak freely with one person but become silent in a group. Another may have ideas in a familiar language and need extra time to organise them in English.

Ask when speaking feels easiest and when it feels difficult. The answer helps separate a language gap from a confidence gap. Both can exist, but they need different support.

Create conversation, not a test

Questions such as “What did you do at school?” are broad and easy to answer with “nothing.” Try questions with a clear starting point:

  • What was the first thing you did after arriving?
  • Which part of the lesson was easiest to understand?
  • If you could change one rule in a game, what would you change?
  • Show me something you made, then tell me how you made it.

Follow the child’s answer rather than moving immediately to the next question. A real conversation includes curiosity, surprise and shared stories from the adult too.

Model the correction without interrupting

If a child says, “Yesterday I go to shop,” the adult can reply, “You went to the shop yesterday. What did you buy?” The correct form is heard, but the conversation continues. Stopping after every error to demand repetition can make a child monitor each word so closely that fluency disappears.

Choose corrections carefully. If the same error repeatedly makes meaning unclear, practise it later through a short game or example. During storytelling, protect the flow.

Fluency develops when children discover that communication can survive an imperfect sentence.

Use stories as a bridge

Stories provide characters, actions and language worth borrowing. After reading, ask the child to choose a favourite moment, change the ending or speak as one character. Family photographs and wordless picture books work especially well because the child is not trying to remember an official answer.

A child can first retell a story with support: “Who was there? Where were they? What happened first?” Over time, remove the prompts. This develops sequence, detail and the confidence to hold another person’s attention.

Let play carry the language

Role-play a shop, restaurant, classroom, doctor’s visit or bus journey. Give the child a purpose: order a meal, ask for directions, explain a problem or welcome a visitor. Repeating useful language inside different games makes it flexible.

Older primary children may prefer guessing games, simple debates, interviews or explaining how to make something. The activity should be interesting enough that English becomes the tool, not the entire point.

Build a small daily routine

Ten minutes is enough to begin

  1. Choose one photograph, object or event.
  2. Let the child speak for one minute without interruption.
  3. Ask two genuine follow-up questions.
  4. Introduce one useful word or phrase.
  5. Use that phrase once more before the conversation ends.

Consistency is more valuable than a long session once a week. Stop while the activity still feels successful. The aim is to make speaking a normal part of family life, not another subject that appears only when homework begins.

Work with the teacher

Share what you observe: where the child speaks comfortably, situations that cause hesitation and interests that produce more language. Ask how speaking is supported in pairs, groups and whole-class activities. A quiet child may first need a prepared sentence with one partner before addressing a larger group.

Celebrate specific growth: asking a question independently, explaining a game, speaking loudly enough to be heard or continuing after forgetting a word. “You kept going even when that sentence was difficult” builds a more useful kind of confidence than “Your English is perfect.”

Respect every language the child knows

English confidence does not require embarrassment about Sinhala, Tamil or another home language. Children should experience multilingual ability as a strength. Families can discuss a complex idea in the language that allows the richest thinking, then explore how to express part of it in English.

Princeway College uses English-medium teaching in its kindergarten and primary programme. Families can explore the school’s approach on the programmes page or contact the school with questions.

Language development varies between children. If a child has persistent difficulty communicating in every language or setting, seek advice from an appropriately qualified professional.
